1987-01-03.title: John Lewis begins service in the U.S. House
paragraphs: John Lewis took his seat in Congress in January 1987, representing Georgia’s Fifth District. He brought to Washington the experience of a movement organizer who had led sit-ins, Freedom Rides, and voting-rights campaigns, and who had been beaten on Bloody Sunday in Selma.

In Congress, Lewis used his office to press for voting access and civil rights, carrying the movement’s demands into federal lawmaking. He served the Atlanta district for more than three decades and became widely known as the “conscience of Congress.”

image.creator: U.S. House of Representatives
image.rights: Public domain, official U.S. government portrait; retain attribution.
image.alt: Official portrait of Congressman John Lewis

1969-01-06.title: Ludie Clay Andrews dies
paragraphs: Ludie Clay Andrews spent her career training Black nurses in a state that denied them equal professional standing. After graduating from Spelman’s nursing program, she led hospital training programs and helped organize Grady Hospital’s Municipal Training School for Colored Nurses.

Andrews challenged Georgia’s licensing barriers for nearly a decade, refusing a special exception that would have benefited only her. Her campaign helped open the state examination to qualified Black nurses, and she became Georgia’s first Black registered nurse. She was buried at South-View.

image.creator: Georgia Women of Achievement (biography page; portrait image rights not stated)
image.rights: No-cleared-portrait. The archive/biography page is a source to request permission; use a clearly labeled nursing-school context image until cleared.
image.alt: Portrait of Ludie Clay Andrews; permission required before reuse

1994-01-10.title: John Wesley Dobbs Avenue is dedicated
paragraphs: Atlanta renamed Houston Street as John Wesley Dobbs Avenue in 1994, honoring a leader who had spent decades building Black political power in the city. Dobbs worked as a railway mail clerk, organized voter-registration drives, and helped found the Atlanta Negro Voters League with attorney A. T. Walden.

The new name placed Dobbs’s legacy directly in Sweet Auburn, the Black business and civic district he helped strengthen. Organizing by Dobbs and his allies helped secure Atlanta’s first Black police officers in 1948 and showed how voter participation could change city policy under segregation.

image.creator: Ralph Helmick (sculpture); Wikimedia Commons record
image.rights: No verified portrait reuse license. Use only after confirming the Commons file’s current license; otherwise use an attributed Sweet Auburn streetscape with its own cleared license.
image.alt: John Wesley Dobbs memorial sculpture in Sweet Auburn; portrait rights require verification

1929-01-15.title: Martin Luther King Jr. is born in Atlanta
paragraphs: Martin Luther King Jr. was born Michael King Jr. at his family’s home on Auburn Avenue in Atlanta. He grew up in Ebenezer Baptist Church, where his father and grandfather were ministers, within a thriving Black neighborhood shaped by both segregation and independent institutions.

King became a Baptist minister and a national civil-rights leader through the Montgomery bus boycott, the Southern Christian Leadership Conference, and campaigns against segregation and disfranchisement. His Atlanta upbringing connected his public leadership to a local tradition of Black education, church life, and civic organizing.

image.creator: New York World-Telegram and Sun staff photographer; Library of Congress collection
image.rights: Public domain in the United States; work-for-hire image, LoC reports no known restrictions.
image.alt: Portrait of Martin Luther King Jr.

1969-01-15.title: South-View holds memorial for Martin Luther King Jr.
paragraphs: On what would have been Martin Luther King Jr.’s 40th birthday, mourners gathered at South-View, where he had been buried after his 1968 assassination. The cemetery became an early site of public remembrance, before King’s remains were moved to the King Center in 1977.

The gathering joined a national birthday observance to the Atlanta community that had shaped King’s life. South-View’s memorial landscape held the graves of movement figures and families alike, making the cemetery a place where private grief and public history met.

image.creator: Photographer unidentified; National Museum of African American History and Culture collection
image.rights: Rights status not specified in the catalog; request permission. The catalog image depicts visitors at King’s original South-View gravesite and is a strong event-specific candidate.
image.alt: Visitors at Martin Luther King Jr.’s original grave at South-View Cemetery

1983-01-15.title: Graham W. Jackson Sr. dies
paragraphs: Graham Washington Jackson Sr. was an Atlanta musician, bandleader, and music educator whose performances ranged from jazz and popular music to church and civic events. He led the Seminole Syncopators and taught music at Booker T. Washington High School, building a career during segregation when Black musicians often faced barriers to venues and audiences.

Jackson became nationally remembered for playing “Goin’ Home” on accordion as Franklin D. Roosevelt’s funeral train left Warm Springs in April 1945. The image of the musician weeping beside the track joined a local friendship with the president to the country’s mourning at the end of wartime leadership.

image.creator: Atlanta History Center / archival photographer; catalog record
image.rights: No-cleared-portrait. Request permission from the holding archive; the famous Ed Clark funeral photograph is copyrighted and should not be reused without a license.
image.alt: Graham W. Jackson Sr.; archival portrait permission required

1933-01-25.title: Dinah Watts Pace dies
paragraphs: Dinah Watts Pace was born enslaved in Georgia and went on to graduate from Atlanta University in 1883. She traveled to Covington to teach Black children, but stayed after seeing how much the community needed schooling and support for children without parents.

Pace built a school and children’s home that educated and cared for hundreds of young people over several decades. Her work combined teaching with daily community care at a time when segregated public resources for Black families were scarce. She died in Atlanta in 1933 and was buried at South-View.

image.creator: Portrait published in Lawson Andrew Scruggs, Women of Distinction (1893)
image.rights: Public domain; published in 1893.
image.alt: Historical portrait of educator Dinah Watts Pace

1992-02-08.title: Bazoline E. Usher dies
paragraphs: Bazoline Estelle Usher spent more than four decades teaching Black students in Atlanta’s segregated schools. She became principal at several schools and, in 1944, the city’s director and supervisor of Negro schools—the highest school-system post then held by a Black educator.

Usher also widened opportunities beyond the classroom: in 1943 she organized Girl Scout troops for Black girls, at a time when many youth programs excluded them. Her career shows how Black educators built institutions and leadership for children despite unequal public systems.

image.creator: Library of Congress, Prints and Photographs Division
image.rights: Public domain in the United States; published before 1931.
image.alt: Archival portrait of educator Bazoline Estelle Usher

1886-02-20.title: Atlanta paper reports Black community buying a cemetery
paragraphs: In February 1886, Atlanta’s Black businessmen organized to buy land for a cemetery of their own. Families had encountered segregated burial grounds and degrading treatment; South-View offered a place where Black Atlantans could bury loved ones with dignity and govern the grounds themselves.

The reported down payment and purchase of acreage marked the practical beginning of the institution. The founders’ effort was part of a broader post-Reconstruction movement to build Black-owned churches, schools, businesses, and mutual-aid organizations in the face of Jim Crow.

image.creator: Unidentified photographer; Library of Congress collection
image.rights: Public domain in the United States; historic photograph published before 1931. It is an unidentified Georgia cemetery, not South-View; label as illustrative.
image.alt: Unidentified historic Georgia cemetery, used as an illustrative image

1940-02-21.title: John Lewis is born
paragraphs: John Robert Lewis was born on a sharecropper’s farm near Troy, Alabama, to a family of tenant farmers. As a young man he heard Martin Luther King Jr. on the radio, studied at American Baptist Theological Seminary and Fisk University in Nashville, and joined the student campaign against segregation.

Lewis became chairman of SNCC, one of the central student-led organizations of the civil-rights movement. He helped organize Freedom Rides and voting campaigns, endured repeated arrests and beatings, and later represented Atlanta in Congress from 1987 until his death.

image.creator: U.S. House of Representatives
image.rights: Public domain, official U.S. government portrait; retain attribution.
image.alt: Official portrait of John Lewis

1903-02-22.title: Graham W. Jackson Sr. is born
paragraphs: Graham Washington Jackson Sr. grew into one of Atlanta’s best-known musicians, performing on organ, piano, and accordion and leading the Seminole Syncopators. He also taught music at Booker T. Washington High School, where Black students built cultural institutions within a segregated school system.

Jackson’s friendship with Franklin D. Roosevelt brought him to Warm Springs, where he performed for the president and was present when Roosevelt died in 1945. His accordion performance at the funeral procession became a lasting image of grief shared by a Black Georgian and a president who had been an important, though complicated, figure in Black Americans’ lives.

image.creator: Atlanta History Center / archival photographer; catalog record
image.rights: No-cleared-portrait. Request archive permission; do not reuse Ed Clark’s famous copyrighted funeral image without a license.
image.alt: Archival portrait of Graham W. Jackson Sr.; permission required

1908-02-22.title: Annie L. McPheeters is born
paragraphs: Annie Lou McPheeters became a librarian when Atlanta’s public library system was racially segregated. At Auburn Branch, she built a Negro History Collection, expanded adult education, and helped Black patrons find books and historical sources that mainstream institutions often overlooked.

McPheeters treated the branch as a civic classroom as well as a library: programs introduced readers to history, public affairs, and voting. She later joined Georgia State University as its first Black faculty member and left papers that document the intellectual life of Black Atlanta.

image.creator: Auburn Avenue Research Library / archival photographer
image.rights: No-cleared-portrait. Archive record provides no explicit reuse license; request permission before publication.
image.alt: Portrait of librarian Annie L. McPheeters; archive permission required

1965-03-07.title: Bloody Sunday in Selma
paragraphs: John Lewis and Hosea Williams led hundreds of voting-rights marchers out of Selma on March 7, 1965. At the Edmund Pettus Bridge, Alabama state troopers and local officers ordered them back, then attacked the unarmed crowd with clubs and tear gas. Lewis suffered a fractured skull.

The march had been planned after police killed voting-rights activist Jimmie Lee Jackson in nearby Marion. Images of the assault—soon known as Bloody Sunday—spread across the country and strengthened pressure for federal protection of Black voting rights; Congress passed the Voting Rights Act later that year.

image.creator: U.S. House of Representatives
image.rights: Public domain, official U.S. government portrait; this is a portrait of Lewis, not a photograph of Bloody Sunday.
image.alt: Official portrait of John Lewis, leader of the Bloody Sunday march

1886-03-18.title: First reported burials at South-View
paragraphs: Within weeks of the founders’ land purchase, South-View was already receiving burials. An Atlanta newspaper reported that ten or twelve people had been buried there, showing how urgently Black families needed a burial ground they could use on their own terms.

The early cemetery grew out of resistance to discriminatory treatment at existing grounds. Its founders created a Black-owned association that could hold land, set its own practices, and offer families a dignified place for mourning and remembrance.

image.creator: Unidentified photographer; Library of Congress collection
image.rights: Public domain in the United States; historic photograph published before 1931. It is not verified as South-View; label as illustrative.
image.alt: Unidentified historic Georgia cemetery, illustrative rather than a photograph of South-View

1904-03-31.title: Harriet Graham dies, prompting a suspicious-death inquiry
paragraphs: Harriet Graham, widow of South-View founder George W. Graham, died unexpectedly at her Atlanta home in 1904. A coroner’s inquiry followed after an anonymous threat raised suspicion, bringing the family’s loss into public view.

The account preserved in South-View’s cemetery history does not establish who, if anyone, caused her death, and the case remained unresolved. Her story sits within the life of a Black community whose founders were building institutions and property ownership amid the insecurity and racial violence of Jim Crow Atlanta.

sources.label: City of the Dead
sources.note: D. L. Henderson, South-View: City of the Dead, chapter 15, OCR page estimate 174 (printed page near 159).

1904-03-31.dateNote: The coroner inquiry and anonymous threat are reported in South-View: City of the Dead (chapter 15); no independent online confirmation found. The article avoids inferring cause or intent.

image.rights: Public domain in the United States; not a portrait of Harriet Graham or a verified view of South-View. Label as illustrative.
image.alt: Unidentified historic Georgia cemetery, used as a general cemetery illustration

1904-04-03.title: Harriet Graham is buried at South-View
paragraphs: Harriet Graham was buried at South-View on Easter Sunday, shortly after her sudden death. Her husband, George W. Graham, had helped establish the cemetery, so her burial joined a family story to the institution he and other Black Atlanta leaders had created.

A coroner had reopened the case after an anonymous threat came to light, but no confirmed explanation for Harriet’s death emerged. The uncertainty should remain part of the story rather than be turned into a claim of murder.

sources.label: City of the Dead
sources.note: D. L. Henderson, South-View: City of the Dead, chapter 15, OCR page estimate 175 (printed page near 160).

1904-04-03.dateNote: The burial date and Easter Sunday detail are reported in South-View: City of the Dead (chapter 15); not independently confirmed online.

image.rights: Public domain in the United States; not a verified image of South-View. Label as illustrative.
image.alt: Unidentified historic Georgia cemetery, used as an illustrative image

1968-04-04.title: Martin Luther King Jr. is assassinated
paragraphs: Martin Luther King Jr. was shot on the balcony of the Lorraine Motel in Memphis on April 4, 1968. He had come to support striking Black sanitation workers and was preparing for another march, continuing his work on labor rights and economic justice as well as racial equality.

King’s assassination brought grief and protest across the country. In Atlanta, thousands joined his funeral procession, and he was first buried at South-View before his remains were moved to the King Center years later.

image.creator: New York World-Telegram and Sun staff photographer; Library of Congress collection
image.rights: Public domain in the United States; work-for-hire image, LoC reports no known restrictions.
image.alt: Portrait of Martin Luther King Jr.

1945-04-13.title: Graham W. Jackson performs at FDR’s funeral procession
paragraphs: The day after Franklin D. Roosevelt died at Warm Springs, Atlanta musician Graham W. Jackson played “Goin’ Home” on his accordion as the president’s funeral train departed. Jackson had performed for Roosevelt before and was personally grieving; photographer Ed Clark captured him in tears beside the tracks.

The photograph became an enduring image of the country’s loss, but it also records a particular relationship: a Black musician from Georgia mourning a president who had opened some federal opportunities to Black Americans while leaving segregation and many racial injustices intact.

image.creator: Ed Clark, Life magazine / Getty Images
image.rights: Copyrighted photograph. Do not use without a license; request permission from Getty/rights holder. Use a separately cleared archival portrait of Jackson instead.
image.alt: Graham W. Jackson playing accordion at Roosevelt’s funeral train; image use requires license

1886-04-21.title: South-View Cemetery charter approved
paragraphs: Georgia approved the South-View Cemetery Association’s charter on April 21, 1886. The charter gave Black founders a legal organization through which they could hold and manage cemetery land, turning a community response to discriminatory burial practices into a lasting institution.

South-View’s incorporation was part of a wider effort by Black Atlantans to build institutions under segregation. Its founders secured collective control over burial, property, and remembrance at a time when those forms of authority were often denied to them.

image.creator: Unidentified photographer; Library of Congress collection
image.rights: Public domain in the United States; not verified as South-View. Label as illustrative.
image.alt: Historic Georgia cemetery, illustrative image and not identified as South-View

1900-05-06.title: Henry Rutherford Butler calls for cemetery beautification
paragraphs: Atlanta physician Henry Rutherford Butler urged South-View lot owners to keep graves “green and clean,” making cemetery care a shared responsibility. His appeal treated the grounds as more than a burial place: careful upkeep honored the dead and affirmed the community’s stewardship of its own institution.

Butler was a physician, civic leader, and advocate for Black Atlanta. South-View’s ongoing care relied on families and community members, whose labor preserved family plots and public dignity in a segregated city.
1900-05-06.dateNote: The May 6 appeal and quotation are reported in South-View: City of the Dead (chapter 6); online sources document Butler’s broader civic and medical work, not this column.

image.creator: Courtesy of Archives Division, Auburn Avenue Research Library, as credited by New Georgia Encyclopedia
image.rights: No-cleared-portrait. The New Georgia Encyclopedia says the archive holds image rights and permission is required; use only after archive clearance.
image.alt: Portrait of physician Henry Rutherford Butler; permission required

1902-05-17.title: Pittsburgh riot kills Black residents in Atlanta
paragraphs: A white mob attacked Atlanta’s Pittsburgh neighborhood south of downtown in 1902, killing Black residents and terrorizing families in the area. The community was home to Black workers and families living amid segregation and repeated threats to their safety.

South-View’s burial history names Will Richardson, James Harrison, and Milton Risdon among the Black victims, but independent records have not confirmed the casualty details. The violence belongs to Atlanta’s wider history of racial terror, often minimized or poorly documented.

sources.label: City of the Dead
sources.note: D. L. Henderson, South-View: City of the Dead, chapter 11, section “The Pittsburgh Riot,” OCR page estimate 130–134 (printed pages around 116–119).

1902-05-17.dateNote: The precise date, victim names, and casualty numbers come from South-View: City of the Dead (chapter 11). Search found no independent online confirmation of the book’s 1902 event details; avoid presenting numbers as independently established.

image.creator: The Atlanta Constitution
image.rights: Public domain; newspaper page published in 1906. This depicts the separate 1906 Atlanta massacre, not the 1902 Pittsburgh incident; label as context only.
image.alt: Front page of the Atlanta Constitution from 1906, contextual image of later racial violence in Atlanta

1940-05-17.title: Henry Ossian Flipper is interred at South-View
paragraphs: Henry Ossian Flipper, born enslaved in Thomasville, became the first African American to graduate from West Point in 1877. He served as an Army officer and engineer, endured isolation and racism at the academy, and was dismissed from the Army after a court-martial whose fairness was later challenged.

Flipper died in Atlanta in 1940 and was buried at South-View before his remains were later moved to his family cemetery in Thomasville. His career opened a path into the military for Black Americans even as the Army maintained segregation and he faced institutional discrimination.

sources.label: City of the Dead
sources.note: D. L. Henderson, South-View: City of the Dead, chapter 11, OCR page estimate 128.

image.creator: Photographer unknown; image from Miriam Matthews Photograph Collection, UCLA Library Digital Collections
image.rights: Commons file page requires a fresh license check; verify rights before publishing.
image.alt: Studio portrait of Henry Ossian Flipper in military uniform

1915-05-19.title: Bishop Henry McNeal Turner is buried at South-View
paragraphs: Henry McNeal Turner’s funeral drew an enormous crowd in Atlanta. A minister, Civil War chaplain, Reconstruction-era legislator, and bishop of the African Methodist Episcopal Church, Turner had spent decades organizing Black churches and arguing for political rights and self-determination.

Turner helped expand the AME Church across the South after emancipation and became one of Georgia’s most influential Black leaders. The thousands who followed his funeral procession to South-View reflected the reach of his religious and political work across generations.
1915-05-19.dateNote: The May 19 burial date is reported in South-View: City of the Dead (chapter 11); article omits unverified attendance figures.

image.creator: Harper’s Weekly, 1863; Library of Congress Prints and Photographs Division
image.rights: No known restrictions on publication per Library of Congress record.
image.alt: 1863 wood engraving portrait of Reverend Henry McNeal Turner

1888-05-22.title: Founders transfer cemetery land to the Association
paragraphs: In 1888, founders transferred about 25 acres to the South-View Cemetery Association, placing the land under the organization’s control. The transaction followed the cemetery’s 1886 charter and helped secure the grounds as a community institution rather than a temporary burial site.

Collective ownership mattered in a city where Black families had faced restrictions and humiliation at white-controlled cemeteries. South-View gave its founders and members a way to shape burial practices, preserve family plots, and expand a Black-led institution over time.

sources.label: City of the Dead
sources.note: D. L. Henderson, South-View: City of the Dead, chapter 4, OCR page estimate 38.

1888-05-22.dateNote: The transaction date and price are reported in South-View: City of the Dead (chapter 4); linked sources establish cemetery founders and ownership context.

image.rights: Public domain in the United States; not verified as South-View. Label as illustrative.
image.alt: Unidentified historic Georgia cemetery, illustrative view

1963-06-12.title: John Wesley Dobbs monument dedicated at South-View
paragraphs: Atlanta’s Prince Hall Masons and Eastern Stars dedicated a broken-column monument at John Wesley Dobbs’s grave in 1963. Dobbs had served as grand master of Georgia’s Prince Hall Masons for three decades and was a leading organizer in Sweet Auburn.

Dobbs also helped build Black political influence through voter registration and the Atlanta Negro Voters League. The monument honored a civic life that linked fraternal service, neighborhood leadership, and the long struggle for political voice under segregation.
1963-06-12.dateNote: The monument dedication date and ceremony participants are reported in South-View: City of the Dead (chapter 10); linked sources support Dobbs’s broader history.

image.creator: Ralph Helmick (sculpture); Wikimedia Commons record

1992-06-17.title: Grace Towns Hamilton dies
paragraphs: Grace Towns Hamilton joined the Atlanta Urban League in 1943 and spent years working on housing, schools, health care, and voter registration. The educator and civic leader built coalitions across Atlanta while challenging the limits segregation placed on Black residents.

In 1966 she became the first Black woman elected to Georgia’s General Assembly and served for nearly two decades. Hamilton’s legislative work expanded Black political representation and linked local civil-rights organizing to state policy; she was buried at South-View.

image.creator: Boyd Lewis Photograph Collection, Kenan Research Center, Atlanta History Center
image.rights: Archive page contains Hamilton portraits but does not state an open reuse license. Request permission from Atlanta History Center before use.
image.alt: Grace Towns Hamilton in the Georgia House; archive permission required

1858-06-26.title: Alonzo Herndon is born
paragraphs: Alonzo Franklin Herndon was born enslaved in Walton County, Georgia. After emancipation he worked as a laborer and learned barbering; in Atlanta he built a successful chain of barbershops serving the city’s Black professional class.

In 1905 Herndon acquired a small mutual-aid insurer and developed it into Atlanta Life Insurance Company, one of the nation’s major Black-owned businesses. The company sold protection to Black families excluded by many white insurers and became a source of jobs, investment, and civic support in segregated Atlanta.

image.creator: Sweet Auburn collection / Wikimedia Commons file record
image.rights: Public domain in the United States according to the Wikimedia Commons file record; the original photographer is unidentified. Source credit: Sweet Auburn / Atlanta Life.
image.alt: Portrait of Atlanta entrepreneur Alonzo Herndon

1933-07-01.title: Jean Childs Young is born
paragraphs: Jean Childs was born in Marion, Alabama, in 1933. She became an educator and civil-rights participant, later joining voter-registration work, the Selma march, and the Poor People’s Campaign.

After marrying Andrew Young, she helped shape education and children’s-rights work at home and nationally. As Atlanta’s first lady in the 1980s, she organized programs that connected young people with college and career opportunities.

image.creator: National Park Service (page image attribution not stated)
image.rights: NPS page is an official government resource; image-specific photographer/rights not stated. Verify before reuse.
image.alt: Jean Childs Young, educator, civil-rights participant, and advocate for children.

1983-07-06.title: Atlanta declares T. J. Flanagan Day
paragraphs: Atlanta City Council honored Thomas Jefferson Flanagan with a city day in 1983, recognizing a career that joined ministry, poetry, painting, and Black journalism. Flanagan wrote for the Atlanta Independent and Atlanta Daily World and published verse including The Road to Mount McKeithan.

His life bridged several institutions of Black Atlanta: the AME pulpit, the historically Black Atlanta University, and the city’s independent press. He was also a longtime railway mail clerk, building a literary and artistic career alongside paid work.
1983-07-06.dateNote: The city-day date is taken from the cemetery-history account; the obituary and archive independently support Flanagan’s career and death in 1983.

image.rights: Archive record has no explicit open reuse license; obtain permission before publishing portrait.
image.alt: Thomas Jefferson Flanagan, Atlanta poet, minister, artist, and newspaper columnist.

2020-07-17.title: John Lewis dies
paragraphs: John Lewis died in Atlanta on July 17, 2020, at age 80. His life had carried him from organizing student sit-ins and Freedom Rides to leading the Student Nonviolent Coordinating Committee and representing Georgia in Congress for 17 terms.

Lewis had been beaten during the 1961 Freedom Rides and again on Bloody Sunday in Selma in 1965. He kept returning to nonviolent organizing and voting rights, insisting that ordinary people could change the country through disciplined collective action.

image.creator: U.S. House of Representatives
image.rights: Public domain, U.S. government work.
image.alt: John Lewis in his official 2003 congressional portrait.

1927-07-21.title: Alonzo Herndon dies
paragraphs: Alonzo Herndon died in Atlanta in 1927, having become one of the city’s wealthiest Black residents. Born enslaved in Georgia, he learned barbering after emancipation, built a chain of prosperous shops, and invested in Atlanta property.

In 1905 he bought a struggling mutual-aid society and developed it into Atlanta Life Insurance Company, which served Black customers often excluded by white insurers. Herndon’s story shows how Black-owned businesses built financial security and civic influence amid Jim Crow.
1927-07-21.dateNote: The exact death date is in the supplied cemetery chronology; NGE and LoC confirm the biography and year.

image.rights: Public domain in the United States according to the Wikimedia Commons file record; the original photographer is unidentified. Source credit: Sweet Auburn / Atlanta Life.

1887-07-26.title: Rev. William R. Clemmons dies after violent assault
paragraphs: William R. Clemmons, pastor of Atlanta’s Mount Olivet Baptist Church, died after a violent assault in 1887. The account of his final days describes church members gathering at his home and congregation, making the violence a loss felt across the community.

Black churches in Reconstruction-era Atlanta were more than places of worship: they organized education, mutual aid, political life, and community care. Clemmons’s ministry belonged to a generation building institutions while Black Atlantans faced racial violence and fragile legal protection.
1887-07-26.dateNote: The assault and exact date come from the supplied cemetery narrative; no independent archival corroboration of the incident was located. The cemetery image is only an illustration.

image.rights: Public domain in the United States (published before 1931); image depicts an unidentified Georgia cemetery, not South-View.

1940-08-01.title: Benjamin E. Mays is appointed president of Morehouse
paragraphs: Benjamin E. Mays took office as Morehouse College president in 1940. A Baptist minister and scholar raised in South Carolina by parents who had been enslaved, he had studied at Bates College and the University of Chicago before becoming dean of Howard’s School of Religion.

Mays led Morehouse for 27 years, building its academic standing and urging students to confront injustice as a public responsibility. Martin Luther King Jr., who entered Morehouse in 1944, later called Mays his spiritual mentor; Mays’s teaching helped shape a generation of Black civic leadership.

1893-08-07.title: South-View trustees seek relief from city license fee
paragraphs: During the economic panic of 1893, South-View’s trustees asked Atlanta to waive a $100 license fee, explaining that many of the cemetery’s burials served people who could not afford more. The petition captures the cemetery’s role as both a community institution and a business struggling to keep burial accessible.

South-View had been founded in 1886 by Black Atlantans who objected to discriminatory treatment at segregated burial grounds. Its joint-stock structure helped the community control land, care for the dead, and preserve dignity when public institutions offered unequal service.
1893-08-07.dateNote: The petition date and amount come from the supplied cemetery chronology; the linked histories support the cemetery’s founding purpose and structure.

image.rights: Public domain in the United States (published before 1931); image depicts an unidentified Georgia cemetery, not South-View.

1963-08-28.title: John Lewis speaks at the March on Washington
paragraphs: At 23, John Lewis spoke at the 1963 March on Washington as chair of SNCC, representing a student movement that had organized sit-ins, Freedom Rides, and voter-registration campaigns. His speech challenged the country to make the promise of freedom real for Black Americans.

The march brought roughly a quarter-million people to the Lincoln Memorial to demand jobs and civil rights. Lewis’s address placed youth-led direct action beside the broader coalition pressing Congress and the Kennedy administration to confront segregation.

image.creator: U.S. House of Representatives
image.rights: Public domain, U.S. government work.
image.alt: John Lewis in his official 2003 congressional portrait.

1961-08-30.title: John Wesley Dobbs dies
paragraphs: John Wesley Dobbs died in Atlanta in 1961, the same week the city’s public schools began desegregating. Known as the “Mayor of Auburn Avenue,” he spent decades organizing Black voters while working as a railway mail clerk.

Dobbs co-founded the Atlanta Negro Voters League with attorney A. T. Walden. Their registration campaigns helped turn Black Atlanta’s growing electorate into political leverage, contributing to reforms such as the hiring of the city’s first Black police officers in 1948.

image.rights: Portrait identified in archive; no reuse license stated on item page. Request permission before publication.

1994-09-16.title: Jean Childs Young dies
paragraphs: Jean Childs Young died in 1994 after a life spent teaching and advocating for children. She worked in civil-rights campaigns, helped develop citizenship education for the Southern Christian Leadership Conference, and took part in major demonstrations from the Selma march to the Poor People’s Campaign.

Young made children’s welfare a public issue, chairing the U.S. Committee for UNICEF and serving as a leading advocate during the International Year of the Child. In Atlanta, she built education and youth programs that continued after Andrew Young’s mayoral years.

image.creator: National Park Service (page image attribution not stated)
image.rights: NPS page is an official government resource; image-specific photographer/rights not stated. Verify before reuse.
image.alt: Jean Childs Young, educator, civil-rights participant, and advocate for children.

1980-09-26.title: Angel monument falls at South-View
paragraphs: A stone angel on the Brown family lot reportedly toppled at South-View on September 26, 1980. Cemetery historian Albert Watts later noted that the fall coincided with the death of Virginia Berry, a family member; the timing became part of the cemetery’s oral history, not evidence of a supernatural cause.

Monuments in historic cemeteries carry family memory in public view. South-View’s range of markers—from elaborate sculpture to simple concrete stones—also reflects differences in wealth and the community’s long effort to honor Black lives across social class.

1967-10-07.title: Ruby Doris Smith Robinson dies
paragraphs: Ruby Doris Smith Robinson died of cancer at 25, after giving years of work to the Student Nonviolent Coordinating Committee. A Spelman student from Atlanta, she joined sit-ins, endured jail and a chain gang in Rock Hill, and later served as SNCC’s administrative secretary.

In 1966 she became SNCC’s executive secretary, the only woman elected to its executive committee. She kept the organization’s Atlanta office connected to field organizers across the South, helping sustain campaigns during a period of intense repression and internal change.

1905-10-10.title: Amos Rucker dies
paragraphs: Amos Rucker, born enslaved and later a resident of Atlanta, died in 1905 at age 81. The cemetery account records him among the people buried at South-View, where burial records preserve names and dates that formal public histories often leave out.

Claims that Rucker served in the Civil War are disputed, so the safest account centers on the documented life arc: a man born before emancipation who lived through Reconstruction and Jim Crow. South-View’s records help recover such individual histories from the city’s Black community.

1905-10-12.title: Amos Rucker is buried at South-View
paragraphs: Amos Rucker was buried at South-View two days after his death. The burial joined one family’s observance to a larger history: the cemetery gave Black Atlantans a burial ground managed by their own community.

Founded in 1886 by formerly enslaved businessmen, South-View became a lasting record of Black Atlanta. Its graves include working people, clergy, educators, entrepreneurs, veterans, and civil-rights leaders, preserving lives that formal public histories often overlook.

sources.label: City of the Dead

1944-10-13.title: Tuskegee Airman Walter Westmoreland is killed in combat
paragraphs: Walter Westmoreland was killed when his aircraft was shot down during an escort mission over Germany on October 13, 1944. He was later buried at South-View, among the veterans whose service is part of the cemetery’s history.

The Tuskegee Airmen were Black U.S. Army Air Forces pilots trained at Tuskegee Army Air Field, supported by ground crews and other military personnel. They flew combat and bomber-escort operations in a segregated military, challenging racist claims used to bar Black Americans from aviation and other military roles.

1964-10-14.title: Martin Luther King Jr. is announced as Nobel Peace Prize laureate
paragraphs: On October 14, 1964, Martin Luther King Jr. was announced as the Nobel Peace Prize laureate. At 35, he became the youngest recipient at the time, recognized for leading nonviolent campaigns against segregation and racial injustice in the United States.

The award came after the Birmingham campaign and the 1963 March on Washington, amid a wider struggle over public accommodations and voting rights. King used the international recognition to draw attention to the movement’s work and accepted the prize in Oslo on December 10.

image.creator: New York World-Telegram and the Sun Newspaper photograph collection, Library of Congress
image.rights: Public domain in the United States; work-for-hire photo in the Library of Congress collection.

1895-10-21.title: John W. E. Bowen delivers “An Appeal to the King”
paragraphs: John Wesley Edward Bowen delivered “An Appeal to the King” during the Cotton States and International Exposition’s Negro Day in Atlanta in October 1895. A theologian and professor, he addressed racial equality in a national showcase that presented the post-Reconstruction South to visitors and investors.

Bowen was the first Black full-time professor at Gammon Theological Seminary. His scholarship and public speaking linked religious education with arguments for Black citizenship, liberal arts learning, and equal participation, even as white political leaders promoted accommodation to segregation.

2015-10-25.title: Sterling Watts is reinterred at South-View
paragraphs: Sterling Watts’s remains were moved from Rest Haven to South-View in 2015. The reinterment returned the elder Watts to the cemetery his son Albert and other Black organizers helped establish, linking a family burial story to a community effort for control over its own dead.

Albert Watts later described watching his father’s burial in a segregated section of Westview Cemetery as a formative humiliation. South-View’s founding answered that experience with a Black-owned cemetery where families could bury loved ones with dignity and maintain their own memorial landscape.

1885-10-26.title: Sterling Watts is buried in segregated Rest Haven
paragraphs: Albert Watts later recalled that his father, Sterling, was buried in Rest Haven, the segregated Black section of Westview Cemetery. He watched the burial through the back gate, an experience the family account remembers as a painful lesson in how segregation governed even mourning.

In 1886 Albert Watts joined other Black businessmen in creating South-View Cemetery. Their project turned a private wound into a lasting institution: a cemetery under Black control that offered families a dignified place to bury loved ones and preserved a record of Atlanta’s Black community.

1904-11-08.title: Horace Mann Bond is born
paragraphs: Horace Mann Bond was born in Nashville in 1904 and became a sociologist, education researcher, and college president. He studied at Lincoln University and the University of Chicago, then led institutions including Fort Valley State College and Lincoln University.

Bond investigated the unequal resources and opportunities facing Black students and supplied research used by the NAACP Legal Defense Fund in the era of Brown v. Board of Education. His work challenged racist claims about Black achievement; he was also the father of civil-rights leader Julian Bond.

1898-11-09.title: Wade Hampton is executed at Atlanta’s new county prison
paragraphs: Wade Hampton was executed at Fulton County’s new prison in Atlanta on November 9, 1898, after a murder conviction. The cemetery narrative describes a public spectacle in which some spectators first watched a circus parade before gathering near the jail.

Hampton was a young Black man tried and executed in a period when the criminal-justice system operated under Jim Crow and racial power was sharply unequal. The event should be presented with the limits of the surviving account in view; modern records have not yet established the trial details or a fuller biography.

1898-11-10.title: Wade Hampton is buried at South-View
paragraphs: After Wade Hampton’s execution, Atlanta undertaker L. L. Lee removed his body, and Hampton was buried at South-View the following day. The interment placed a young man’s grave among generations of Black Atlanta families.

South-View was founded to give Black residents greater control over burial and remembrance in a city shaped by segregated cemeteries. Its records preserve both celebrated public figures and people whose stories survive only through family memory and burial entries.

1927-11-17.title: Lucius Holsey monument is unveiled at South-View
paragraphs: A monument to Bishop Lucius Henry Holsey was unveiled at South-View in 1927, with his five-year-old great-granddaughter participating in the ceremony. It honored a church leader whose influence reached far beyond Atlanta.

Born enslaved in Georgia, Holsey helped organize the Colored Methodist Episcopal Church after emancipation and became one of its bishops in 1873. He built congregations and schools, including Paine College with Methodist partners, and became a major religious and educational leader in Black Georgia.

1955-12-05.title: Montgomery bus boycott begins
paragraphs: On December 5, 1955, Black residents of Montgomery, Alabama, began a mass bus boycott after Rosa Parks was arrested for refusing to surrender her seat to a white passenger. The protest lasted 381 days and ended after the Supreme Court ordered bus segregation unconstitutional.

Martin Luther King Jr., then a young Montgomery pastor, became the boycott’s public spokesman and helped lead the Montgomery Improvement Association. The campaign showed how sustained local organizing, carpools, church networks, and legal action could challenge segregation—and launched King into national leadership.

1886-12-06.title: Charles Morgan buys first South-View association shares
paragraphs: Charles Morgan purchased the first three shares in the South-View Cemetery Association in December 1886, shortly after the cemetery’s founding. His investment helped turn a community demand for dignified burial into an operating institution with land, governance, and a plan for permanence.

Morgan and other formerly enslaved Black businessmen organized South-View because Atlanta’s segregated burial grounds offered unequal treatment. Their cemetery became a rare Black-controlled corporation and a place where families could choose how to honor their dead.

1964-12-10.title: Martin Luther King Jr. receives the Nobel Peace Prize
paragraphs: Martin Luther King Jr. accepted the Nobel Peace Prize in Oslo on December 10, 1964, after being named laureate for his leadership of nonviolent resistance to racial injustice. He was 35, and the award brought worldwide attention to the U.S. civil-rights movement.

King donated the prize money to the movement. In his Nobel lecture, he connected the struggle against segregation to a wider fight against poverty, colonialism, and violence, arguing that nonviolent action could transform public life.

1886-12-17.title: South-View founder Charles Morgan is buried
paragraphs: Charles Morgan died soon after purchasing the first shares in South-View Cemetery Association and was buried in a family lot at the cemetery in December 1886. The founder’s burial connected the new enterprise to the families and leaders who were building it.

South-View’s Black founders set out to make burial a matter of community ownership and dignity. The cemetery’s continuing use across more than a century has preserved the resting places of Atlanta’s clergy, educators, entrepreneurs, veterans, and civil-rights organizers.

1972-12-21.title: Horace Mann Bond dies
paragraphs: Horace Mann Bond died in 1972 after a career as a scholar and college leader. He had served as president of Lincoln University from 1945 to 1957, becoming its first Black and first alumnus president, and also led Fort Valley State College in Georgia.

Bond used social science research to document the barriers facing Black education and to challenge racist theories of intelligence. His scholarship contributed to the environment in which Brown v. Board of Education was argued; his son Julian became a leading civil-rights organizer and Georgia legislator.

1994-12-23.title: Annie L. McPheeters dies
paragraphs: Annie L. McPheeters died in 1994 after a career that opened Atlanta’s libraries to Black readers and researchers. At the Auburn Branch, she created the Negro History Collection, gathering books by and about people of African descent when such material was scarce in public libraries.

McPheeters also built adult-education and children’s programming and helped move the collection to the West Hunter Branch in 1949. She became one of Atlanta’s first Black professional librarians; the city later named a branch and the Auburn Avenue Research Library gallery in her honor.

1885-12-26.title: Bazoline E. Usher is born
paragraphs: Bazoline Estelle Usher was born in Georgia in 1885 and went on to teach generations of Black students in Atlanta’s segregated schools. She earned degrees at Atlanta University and advanced through classroom teaching and school administration.

Usher became Atlanta’s first Black supervisor of its African American schools and the first Black official with an office at City Hall. In 1943 she organized Girl Scout troops for Black girls, expanding access to leadership and recreation while segregation restricted their opportunities.

2012-12-31.title: Lillian Miles Lewis dies
paragraphs: Lillian Miles Lewis died in Atlanta on December 31, 2012. An educator with an international outlook, she served as a Peace Corps volunteer in Nigeria before earning a library-science degree and joining Atlanta University as a librarian in 1965.

Lewis later worked in higher-education administration at Clark Atlanta University and was a trusted adviser to her husband, Congressman John Lewis. Her papers preserve her own career alongside records of their shared public life, giving her a place in the history of Atlanta’s universities and civil-rights networks.

william-h-crogman.name: William H. Crogman
paragraphs: William Henry Crogman was born in Philipsburg on the Caribbean island of Sint Maarten in 1841. After emancipation, he pursued an education in the United States, studied at Claflin University, and joined Atlanta’s Clark University in 1876 to teach Greek and Latin.

Crogman became one of Clark’s most respected scholars and served as its president from 1903 to 1910. He argued for broad liberal-arts education and equal citizenship, using classical learning to challenge the assumption that Black students should receive only narrow vocational training.

grace-towns-hamilton.name: Grace Towns Hamilton
paragraphs: Grace Towns Hamilton was born in Atlanta in 1907 and trained as an educator and social scientist. She led the Atlanta Urban League from 1943 to 1961, directing campaigns that addressed housing, health care, school inequality, and voter registration within the constraints of segregation.

Hamilton entered the Georgia House in 1966 as the first African American woman elected to the state legislature. She served until 1985, working on reapportionment and city-government reform so Black residents could gain fairer representation in public decisions.

alonzo-herndon.name: Alonzo Herndon
paragraphs: Born enslaved in 1858, Alonzo Herndon worked as a farm laborer before learning the barber trade after emancipation. In Atlanta he built a chain of barbershops, including a prominent shop on Peachtree Street that served Black professionals and became a hub of Black business life.

Herndon acquired the Atlanta Benevolent and Protective Association in 1905 and grew it into Atlanta Life Insurance Company. The insurer served Black policyholders turned away by white firms, employed Black professionals, and helped finance civic institutions; Herndon became one of Atlanta’s leading Black businessmen and philanthropists.

annie-l-mcpheeters.name: Annie L. McPheeters
paragraphs: Annie Lou McPheeters trained as a librarian at Hampton and Columbia and began working in Atlanta’s segregated public library system in the 1930s. At Auburn Branch she developed the Negro History Collection and created programs that helped Black readers study history, literature, and public affairs.

McPheeters expanded library service despite separate facilities and unequal resources. She advocated for desegregation, later became the first Black faculty member at Georgia State University, and left papers that preserve the work of Black librarians and readers in Atlanta.

graham-w-jackson-sr.name: Graham W. Jackson Sr.
paragraphs: Graham Washington Jackson Sr. was an Atlanta musician, bandleader, and teacher known for his command of organ, piano, and accordion. He performed with his group the Seminole Syncopators and taught at Booker T. Washington High School, helping shape the city’s Black music scene during segregation.

Jackson became a nationally recognized figure through his friendship with Franklin D. Roosevelt. After Roosevelt died in Warm Springs in 1945, Jackson played “Goin’ Home” on accordion beside the departing funeral train; the photograph of his tears became an image of both personal grief and public mourning.

ludie-clay-andrews.name: Ludie Clay Andrews
paragraphs: Ludie Clay Andrews trained as a nurse at Spelman’s MacVicar Hospital program, graduating in 1906, and became a leader in Georgia’s Black nursing schools. She supervised training programs at Lula Grove Hospital and Grady Hospital and helped prepare generations of nurses to serve Black communities.

Georgia barred Black nurses from its licensing examination, so Andrews spent years challenging the policy and refused an individual exception that would not help other nurses. The state opened registration to qualified Black nurses around 1919–1920, and Andrews became Georgia’s first Black registered nurse.

john-lewis.name: John Lewis
paragraphs: John Lewis grew up on his family’s farm in Alabama and was inspired by the Montgomery bus boycott to join the freedom struggle. A student at Fisk University, he helped found SNCC, became its chairman, took part in the Freedom Rides, and was the youngest speaker at the 1963 March on Washington.

Lewis endured arrests and violence while organizing for voting rights, most famously when troopers beat him on Selma’s Edmund Pettus Bridge on Bloody Sunday in 1965. He later served Atlanta in Congress for 33 years, carrying the movement’s push for equal political participation into national government.

dinah-watts-pace.name: Dinah Watts Pace
paragraphs: Dinah Watts Pace was born enslaved in Georgia in 1853 and later studied at Atlanta University, graduating from its normal department in 1883. She went to Covington to teach, but soon made education and child welfare her life’s work.

Pace founded a school and home for Black children, taking in orphans and educating hundreds over more than forty years. Her institution filled urgent needs in a segregated society where public support was limited; local residents remembered her as a community builder as well as a teacher.

freddye-henderson.name: Freddye Henderson
paragraphs: Freddye Scarborough Henderson was an Atlanta educator, columnist, entrepreneur, and advocate for international travel. In 1955 she and her husband, James, founded Henderson Travel Service, a Black-owned agency that arranged trips for clients who often faced discrimination from mainstream travel companies.

The agency helped African Americans travel abroad during the Jim Crow era, including a 1957 group journey to Ghana for its independence celebrations. Henderson’s work connected business ownership with a wider vision of cultural exchange and mobility for Black travelers.

martin-luther-king-jr.name: Martin Luther King Jr.
paragraphs: Martin Luther King Jr. grew up in Atlanta’s Ebenezer Baptist Church and became a Baptist minister shaped by the Black church, Gandhian nonviolence, and the struggle against segregation. The Montgomery bus boycott made him a national leader, and he later helped build the Southern Christian Leadership Conference to coordinate campaigns across the South.

King’s public work joined desegregation to voting rights, labor, and economic justice. From Birmingham and Selma to Memphis, he urged nonviolent direct action against systems that denied Black Americans equal citizenship; he was assassinated while supporting Memphis sanitation workers in 1968.

benjamin-e-mays.name: Benjamin E. Mays
paragraphs: Benjamin Elijah Mays was born in South Carolina in 1894 to parents who had been enslaved. He studied at Bates College and the University of Chicago, became a Baptist minister and scholar, and served as dean of Howard University’s School of Religion before returning to Atlanta.

As president of Morehouse College from 1940 to 1967, Mays built the school’s academic reputation and urged students to confront injustice. Martin Luther King Jr. later called him his spiritual mentor. After retiring, Mays chaired Atlanta’s school board during desegregation; he was first buried at South-View before reinterment at Morehouse.

jean-childs-young.name: Jean Childs Young
paragraphs: Jean Childs Young was born in Marion, Alabama, in 1933 and trained as a teacher after graduating from Manchester College. She taught in Atlanta and took part in civil-rights activism, including the city’s 1961 lunch-counter campaign, the Selma voting-rights march, and the Poor People’s Campaign.

Young helped develop citizenship education for the Southern Christian Leadership Conference and became a national advocate for children, serving as chair of the U.S. Committee for UNICEF. As Atlanta’s first lady during Andrew Young’s mayoral terms, she created education and career programs for local youth.

horace-mann-bond.name: Horace Mann Bond
paragraphs: Horace Mann Bond was born in Nashville in 1904 and became a sociologist, education researcher, and college administrator. After studying at Lincoln University and the University of Chicago, he led Fort Valley State College in Georgia and later Lincoln University, where he became the first Black and first alumnus president.

Bond documented the unequal resources and opportunities facing Black students and produced research used by the NAACP Legal Defense Fund in the period of Brown v. Board of Education. He wrote about Black education and Pan-Africanism and was the father of civil-rights leader Julian Bond.

bazoline-e-usher.name: Bazoline E. Usher
paragraphs: Bazoline Estelle Usher was born in Georgia in 1885 and spent more than four decades teaching in Atlanta’s segregated public schools. She studied at Atlanta University, became a teacher and principal, and built a reputation as an educator who expected Black students to receive serious academic opportunities.

Usher became Atlanta’s first Black supervisor of African American schools and the first Black official with an office at City Hall. In 1943 she organized Girl Scout troops for Black girls, opening space for leadership and outdoor activities when segregation excluded them from many programs.

lillian-miles-lewis.name: Lillian Miles Lewis
paragraphs: Lillian Miles Lewis was born in Los Angeles in 1939 and developed an international outlook through study, library work, and two years as a volunteer teacher in Nigeria. She earned a master’s degree in library science and joined Atlanta University in 1965 as a librarian and director of special collections.

Lewis continued her work in higher-education administration at Clark Atlanta University and served on Georgia’s State Ethics Commission. She married John Lewis in 1968 and was his close adviser throughout his public career; her papers preserve her own professional work as well as their shared life.

robert-grant.name: Robert Grant
paragraphs: After emancipation, Robert Grant helped build institutions that gave Atlanta’s Black community places to worship and organize. A skilled blacksmith and drayman, he joined seven members of Friendship Baptist Church in founding Zion Hill Baptist Church in 1872. As its first pastor, he organized a deacon board, a mothers’ board, a choir, and Sunday school.

Grant also invested in South-View Cemetery, one of six Black businessmen named in the cemetery association’s charter application in 1886. In a segregated city where Black families were often denied dignified burial options, the cemetery and its founding church represented community ownership and self-determination. Zion Hill’s archival history dates Grant’s pastorate to 1872–1876 and says he died in 1896; a precise birth or death day has not been established.

john-w-dobbs.name: John W. Dobbs
paragraphs: John Wesley Dobbs became one of Atlanta’s most influential Black civic organizers in the decades when Jim Crow laws restricted voting and public life. After leaving Atlanta Baptist College to support his family, he passed a civil-service exam and worked for 32 years as a railway mail clerk. He kept studying on his own and became known around Auburn Avenue as “the Grand” for his leadership in Prince Hall Freemasonry.

Dobbs turned that standing into political organizing. He founded the Atlanta Civic and Political League in 1936 and co-founded the Atlanta Negro Voters League with attorney A. T. Walden in 1946. Their registration drives helped build pressure for Atlanta’s first eight Black police officers in 1948 and streetlights on Auburn Avenue the next year. Dobbs helped popularize “Sweet Auburn,” a name for the Black business and civic district.

moses-amos.name: Dr. Moses Amos
paragraphs: Moses Amos learned pharmacy as an apprentice in Atlanta under druggist J. C. Huss. In the early twentieth century, he became Georgia’s first licensed Black pharmacist, at a time when segregated health care and discrimination limited Black residents’ access to medicines and professional training. He went on to acquire the Auburn Avenue drugstore where he had worked and, in 1914, reopened it as Gate City Drug Store.

Gate City was more than a shop: it served a growing Black neighborhood and became part of Sweet Auburn’s network of Black-owned businesses. Amos hired Black women as clerks, mentored younger pharmacists, and helped make pharmacy a path into health care and entrepreneurship. The business later moved to the West Side under Amos and his nephew, Miles Green Amos.

carolyn-d-yancey.name: Carolyn D. Yancey
paragraphs: Carolyn Dunbar Yancey began her career as a teacher after studying education and social work. Born in Detroit in 1921, she later moved with her family to Atlanta, where she became active in civic organizations and public education. In 1982, voters elected her to the Atlanta Board of Education, where she served for sixteen years.

In 1985, Governor Joe Frank Harris appointed Yancey to the University System of Georgia Board of Regents, making her the first Black woman to serve on that board. Her work placed her in institutions that shaped both public schools and higher education during a period of change in Atlanta. She died in 2010.

geneva-haugabrooks.name: Geneva Haugabrooks
paragraphs: Geneva Moton Haugabrooks turned a small start into a long-running business on Auburn Avenue. After studying at Spelman and working as a teacher, she opened Haugabrooks Funeral Home in 1929 with roughly $300. She became one of Atlanta’s pioneering Black women funeral directors and a familiar figure in the city’s African American community, often called “Ma Haugabrooks.”

The funeral home met a vital need in a segregated city, providing funeral services and helping families honor their dead. Haugabrooks also supported civic, religious, and charitable groups, including Wheat Street Baptist Church, the Urban League, and voter-registration efforts. Her business became a neighborhood institution and remained part of Sweet Auburn’s Black-owned commercial life for decades.

john-w-e-bowen.name: John W. E. Bowen
paragraphs: John Wesley Edward Bowen was a theologian, minister, and educator whose scholarship challenged the racial assumptions of his era. Born in New Orleans in 1855, he studied at New Orleans University and Boston University, where he became one of the first African Americans to earn a Ph.D. He taught at Morgan College and Howard University before joining Gammon Theological Seminary in Atlanta in 1893 as its first full-time Black professor.

Bowen later led Gammon as president and helped train generations of Black clergy. At the 1895 Cotton States and International Exposition, he delivered “An Appeal to the King,” a public argument for Black citizenship and equality. During Atlanta’s 1906 racial violence, Bowen opened Gammon’s campus as a refuge and was himself beaten and arrested. He also edited The Voice of the Negro and wrote on religion, education, and African American life.
